title: Angular Momentum and Moment of Inertia
subcategory: System of Particles and Rotational Motion — Angular Momentum, Moment of Inertia, Rolling

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

summary: Moment of inertia is a body's rotational analogue of mass (resistance to change in rotational motion); angular momentum (L = Iω) is conserved whenever no external torque acts, exactly mirroring linear momentum conservation.
explanation: Moment of inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² measures how a body's mass is distributed relative to an axis of rotation — the farther the mass is from the axis, the larger I, and the harder it is to start or stop rotation about that axis. Unlike mass, I depends on both the amount of matter AND the chosen axis, so the same object has different I values about different axes. Angular momentum L = Iω (or L = r × p for a particle) is the rotational counterpart of linear momentum p = mv. Newton's second law in rotational form is τ = dL/dt: torque changes angular momentum exactly as force changes linear momentum. When net external torque is zero, angular momentum is conserved (L = constant) — this is why a spinning ice skater speeds up when pulling their arms in (I decreases, so ω increases to keep Iω constant) and why planets sweep out equal areas in equal times (Kepler's second law, a direct consequence of angular momentum conservation under gravity's central force). Rolling without slipping combines translation of the COM with rotation about the COM; total kinetic energy is KE = ½mv² + ½Iω², and for rolling, v = ωR links the two. The radius of gyration k is defined by I = Mk², an equivalent single distance from the axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same I.
commonMisconceptions: Treating moment of inertia as a fixed property of an object like mass — it changes with the axis of rotation and with how mass is redistributed (arms in vs. out).
Forgetting the rolling-without-slipping condition v = ωR when combining translational and rotational kinetic energy — using it incorrectly is a very common numerical-problem trap.
Assuming angular momentum conservation requires zero net force — it only requires zero net TORQUE; a net force through the axis produces no torque and still allows L to be conserved.
examples: A figure skater pulling their arms inward spins faster because their moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum stays constant.

A solid sphere rolling down an incline reaches the bottom faster than a hollow sphere of the same mass and radius, because its lower moment of inertia means less kinetic energy is 'used up' in rotation.
genZNote: Pull your arms in, spin faster — angular momentum conservation is basically a built-in cheat code.
